item.title: British Passport Validity in Spain and When to Renew
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
Every British passport has an expiry date printed inside. In Spain, that date can mislead you. Since Brexit, Schengen rules set their own limit, often months earlier. The gap has caught out plenty of British travelers at Spanish airports. Renewing in Spain takes longer than renewing in the UK, leaving less room for error. What Passport Validity Rules Apply When Entering Spain Since January 2021, Spain treats UK passports like any other non-EU passport. Two tests apply on arrival day. Your passport must have been issued less than 10 years before that date and remain valid for at least three months after you plan to leave the Schengen area. Older passports tend to fail the first test. Until September 2018, HM Passport Office carried up to nine unused months from old passports to new ones. Some passports show an expiry date more than 10 years after issue. Schengen ignores those extra months. Take a passport issued in August 2017 that expires in May 2028. For entry into Spain, it stops working in August 2027. The second test depends on the trip. Flying into Málaga for a fortnight? You need three clear months after the return flight, so about three and a half months left on the day you fly out. Short-stay visitors get 90 days in any 180, covering the whole Schengen area. Airline staff check at the desk. Border officers verify again on arrival. Either can stop you. GOV.UK has a passport checker for travel to Europe that runs both tests against your exact travel date, so use it before booking. How the Rules Differ for British Residents in Spain British citizens who lived in Spain before the end of 2020 and registered under the Withdrawal Agreement hold a TIE residence card. The 90/180-day limit does not apply, and border officers should not stamp their passports. People who moved later on a visa, such as the non-lucrative or digital nomad visa, also carry a TIE. A TIE does not make the passport optional. You still need a valid one to travel, and Spanish residency paperwork, including TIE renewals, usually asks to see it. If it expires during an application, the process can stall. Many residents renew about six months early rather than wait for a trip to force the issue. Trips beyond Spain bring their own rules. Indonesia, for one, wants six months of validity on arrival. That's stricter than Schengen. What to Do When Your Passport Is Close to Expiry in Spain Skip the consulate. British consulates in Spain do not issue passports. Every renewal goes through HM Passport Office in the UK, and from Spain there are two main ways to apply. The standard route is the GOV.UK online application for renewing from abroad. You fill in the form and upload a photo, then send the old passport to the UK by post or courier-the new one returns by courier to your address in Spain. While HM Passport Office has your old passport, you cannot travel outside Spain. Delivery time adds to processing time. It is the cheapest option and works well if you have months to spare. The HM Passport Office runs a fast-track service. It is only available in the UK, and applications from abroad follow the standard overseas timeline. Some agents, including ASAP Passports, offer UK passport renewal from Spain and handle the UK side of the application. ASAP Passports is a private, registered UK passport agent. HM Passport Office still issues the passport. DHL collects your old passport from an address in Spain, so no consulate visit is needed. Expect to pay more than the standard passport fee. Most people who use this service have an upcoming flight or residency appointment. What if the trip is days away? Neither route may be quick enough. A British national whose passport has expired or does not meet Schengen requirements can apply for an Emergency Travel Document through GOV.UK. It covers one specific journey. You will still need to renew properly afterward. Start with the earliest date that matters to you. Visitors should check their next entry into Spain and run both Schengen tests against it. Residents usually focus on their next TIE renewal or trip abroad. Then work backward. A standard overseas application needs processing time plus round-trip courier time. A rejected photo or missing document delays everything. Six months covers most delays. With under two months left, you will likely choose between a faster route or new travel dates. Look at the issue date as well. It is easy to miss. If your passport was issued before September 2018 and carries extra months, your Schengen limit is 10 years from issue. That can be almost a year before the printed expiry date. Once the new passport arrives, the number changes. Update it on any flights already booked. Spanish banks holding a copy of your old passport will usually ask for the new one. This article was published in partnership with ASAP Passports.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: What to Expect at International Car Rental Pickup Locations
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
Learn what you'll encounter when picking up a rental car at international locations, from required documents and insurance to vehicle inspection, so you can prepare for a hassle-free experience, whether you're seeking information on how to hire a car in Reykjavik or traveling elsewhere abroad. Landing at an international destination and heading to the car rental desk is a common start to many backpacking and road trip adventures. The pickup procedure can be unfamiliar, and knowing what to expect helps prevent stress and surprises. Whether you are comparing options for how to hire a car in Reykjavik or planning your first rental in another country, understanding the typical sequence at car rental locations and global variations will make your arrival smoother. Your car rental pickup experience usually begins as soon as you clear customs or enter the arrival hall, where most providers have a desk, kiosk, or shuttle. Present your documents, confirm your reservation, sign the agreement, inspect the vehicle, and collect the keys before driving out. Although the core steps are similar worldwide, regional rules and provider procedures can vary, from security deposits to the vehicle inspection process. Airport pickups may differ from downtown or off-site locations, and some countries require extra insurance formalities at pickup. Advance preparation can help prevent common pickup delays. Most car rental companies require a full, valid driver's license in English or an official translation. Many countries require an International Driving Permit if your license is not in Roman characters. You'll also need a passport or national ID, a credit card in the main driver's name, and your reservation confirmation. Paper or digital copies are accepted in many places. Age requirements vary, and travelers under 25 may pay young driver surcharges or face higher deposit holds. Adding extra drivers means presenting their documents and sometimes paying a daily fee. Standard practice is for the rental company to place a security hold or pre-authorization on your card, which can be a substantial sum depending on the vehicle and insurance choices. Make sure your card has enough available credit to avoid disruptions. At the Counter: Handling Paperwork and Options At the desk, staff will verify your details, including identity, license, reservation period, and vehicle class. You'll have an opportunity to review major policies, including: - Mileage policy: Check whether it's unlimited or restricts daily distance. - Fuel policy: Many international rentals require the car to be returned with a full tank, but some operate on other systems (pre-purchase or return empty). - Cross-border travel: Some contracts limit where you can drive; always confirm whether you plan to cross into another country. - Late returns: Understand grace periods and potential charges for missed deadlines. Staff may offer optional extras such as GPS units, child seats, roadside assistance, or premium upgrades. While these can be useful, especially for navigation, consider whether they fit your needs or if you can rely on options such as phone apps. Declining unnecessary extras at the counter helps prevent unanticipated costs later. Insurance and Protection Explained Simply Car rental insurance can be confusing. At pickup, you'll encounter different coverage options: collision damage waiver (CDW), theft protection, personal accident insurance, and third-party liability. Some core protections are included by law or with premium credit cards, but optional add-ons may have exclusions or deductibles. Ask direct questions about what is included with your rate, what the excess (your financial responsibility) is, and what local laws require. Scrutinize the contract for key exclusions, such as coverage that doesn't apply if you're driving on certain roads or if required documents are missing. If you purchased insurance from a third party, confirm with your rental company how claims are handled. Once you have the keys, inspect the car thoroughly before leaving the lot. Note any pre-existing damage, such as scratches, dents, or chips, and check that it is recorded in the rental paperwork. Check tires for adequate tread and inflation, test all lights and indicators, and confirm the wipers and washers work. Look for the spare tire, jack, and emergency kit so you're prepared if anything happens on remote routes. Take time-stamped photos of the car's exterior, interior, odometer, and fuel gauge as proof of the rental's condition at pickup. Spend a minute locating essential controls, such as headlights, hazard lights, defogger, and the parking brake, especially if the layout differs from vehicles in your home country. Before setting off, set up your preferred navigation system and double-check your first destination. Many international airports have complex exits or toll systems. Make sure you understand how local road rules differ, such as roundabout priority or speed signage. Be prepared for unfamiliar payment systems for tolls, parking, and fuel. Some areas use ticket machines or require specific cards. Staff can often explain the basics if you ask at pickup. The return process can go smoothly if you prepare ahead of time. Most companies require you to refuel to the same level as at pickup, usually "full to full." Keep your fuel receipt in case of disputes. Some locations allow after-hours returns using secure key drop boxes. Check your agreement to confirm the procedure. Request a final inspection from staff if available, and ensure they note that the car was returned undamaged and with the correct fuel level and mileage. Keep a copy of the final invoice and any documents for your records in case questions arise after your trip. Avoiding Frequent Mistakes: Quick Checklist for Travelers - Don't skip the vehicle inspection; record any existing damage. - Understand your fuel policy to avoid extra charges. - Check your reservation for pickup times to avoid missing your slot or incurring late fees. - Know how much will be held as a deposit and on which card. - Always confirm driver requirements and rules if sharing driving duties. Screenshot or save this checklist to keep organized and reduce stress at your next international pickup. Some preparation and attention to detail at the counter can help you spend more time exploring on road trips and less time dealing with paperwork. This story was published in partnership with Reykjavík Rent A Car ehf.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Camí Vell De Collbató Al Monestir: Walking up to Montserrat on the Old Camí De La Costa
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
Montserrat is a mountain near Barcelona, Spain, and home to the Abbey of Santa Maria de Montserrat. This hike starts in Collbató and follows the Camí Vell, an old pilgrimage route, past stone waymarks and viewpoints to the monastery. Today we are going up to this old shrine by one of the paths used by legendary pilgrims and hermits who came to venerate the famous Virgin Mary. This is why the place of worship was founded more than a thousand years ago. The Camí de la Costa is a well-known path once used by men, pack animals, and traders to reach Montserrat. Traffic on this route into the mountain mattered so much that even Peter III, king of Aragon, made his pilgrimage to Montserrat along this historic path in 1344. The route starts on Montserrat's southern side, in the old village of Collbató. This place is so extraordinary that even the devil himself took to deceiving the mountain's hermits, and that is where the legend of the famous hermit Fra Garí comes from: he gave in to worldly pleasures after listening to the devil disguised as a holy man. The route starts at El Pujolet in Collbató on the south side of the mountain. If you have a vehicle, you can drive straight there. If coming by bus from Barcelona, choose a Monbus departure that stops inside Collbató village. From there, it's a short walk to the El Pujolet trailhead. km 0 · elevation 407 m (1,335 ft) · suggested start 8:00 a.m. We set off early from El Pujolet. Starting along this legendary path first thing in the morning is pure magic. The first rays of sun stroke the mountain, and the summits begin to take on color. km 2.12 · elevation 571 m (1,874 ft) · elapsed time 23 min 30 s The path is quiet. As I say, it was an old pilgrim way up to the monastery, and the gradients are gentle. On clear days we can make out the Mediterranean in the distance. Little by little we gain height. It is a good idea to go up the mountain as the old ascetics did: in silence, listening to the mountain and its sounds. With luck, you may come across some of its inhabitants. km 3.03 · elevation 719 m (2,359 ft) · elapsed time 36 min 13 s Along the way, at the start and as we go, we see signs showing us that we are on a very old pilgrim route, one still in use today. We walk this fine old path and notice that in many stretches the stone paving still survives. The path was made good so pack animals and traders could reach the Marian monastery of Santa Maria de Montserrat. km 3.50 · elevation 771 m (2,530 ft) · elapsed time 42 min 50 s Almost without noticing, we reach the turn-off towards the Sant Joan sector. We carry on straight and don't take it because we are following the original path, the Camí Vell de Collbató al Monestir. The summits and sharp needles of Montserrat soon appear ahead, showing all their character and coming out to greet us. Around every bend, the mountain gives us a new picture, like a film sequence. 4. Pla dels Soldats (Pla de Sant Miquel) km 5.33 · elevation 850 m (2,789 ft) · elapsed time 1 h 00 min About 18 minutes later we reach the Pla dels Soldats, or Pla de Sant Miquel. Here we leave the southern side and enter the monastery's surroundings. Several paths meet here, such as the Camí de les Ermites and the Camí de Sant Miquel, which we will take. This place mattered greatly to old pilgrims: reaching it meant they could almost breathe the monastery's air. They were very close, like us. km 5.93 · elevation 819 m (2,687 ft) · elapsed time 1 h 05 min We continue along an easy track with the mountain on our left and soon reach the Capella de Sant Miquel. In these parts, long ago, the monastery's Abbot would come out to receive the day's important visitors. km 6.20 · elevation 777 m (2,549 ft) · elapsed time 1 h 14 min · 7-minute detour there and back A little further down, off to one side of the path, we can make a short detour to see one of the most incredible views of the monastery from the famous Creu de Sant Miquel. It is one of the finest views of the monastery and is worth staying a while to enjoy. The Marian monastery of Santa Maria de Montserrat appears in the distance, as if carved out of the rock. Beyond its roofs, crowned by the legendary conglomerate needles of the Tebaida area, la Mòmia (the Mummy), l'Elefant (the Elephant), la Prenyada (the Pregnant One), and a few more stand watch. km 6.57 · elevation 778 m (2,552 ft) · elapsed time 1 h 16 min We carry on, perhaps hearing the bells announcing the eleven o'clock conventual Mass. A lovely holm oak opens ahead and keeps us company for a stretch where shade travels with us as we follow the Camí de Sant Miquel. km 7.00 · elevation 747 m (2,451 ft) · elapsed time 1 h 19 min Shortly after, we pass the Porta de Sant Miquel. From there, sculptures and offerings left by the faithful appear at every step, reminding us of the faith that fills these places. km 7.76 · elevation 723 m (2,372 ft) · elapsed time 1 h 24 min Little by little, we follow this paved road to the monastery's edge. We leave the Way of the Cross path on our left and continue to Placa de l'Abat Oliba, named after the monastery's founder in 1025, where a small church once stood. We pass under the arch of Montserrat and walk the last few meters to the monastery's outer façade, carved from the mountain's stone after the Spanish Civil War. Once in the Placa de Santa Maria, that outer façade stands right in front of us in all its magnificence, and surrounded by the huge conglomerate needles of Montserrat, we are standing in the famous Abbey of Montserrat. Pilgrims as legendary as Saint Ignatius of Loyola got this far; he traded his sword for a pilgrim's habit in March 1522. That is how much Montserrat can change a person. On the façade, below Saint George's feet, you can read the inscription "Catalunya serà cristiana o no serà" (Catalonia will be Christian, or it will not be). This phrase has become a symbol of Catholicism in Catalan society. When you are here, do not forget to turn around: the mountain that holds this monastery, the one behind you, hides a whole area that was declared a natural park on 6 March 1987. The path is straightforward and easy to follow. The Patronat de la Muntanya de Montserrat has signs at key points to show hikers which way to go. Once you are near the monastery, at the Pla dels Soldats, the way in is impossible to miss. Even so, it is always sensible to follow the route on a navigation device. We will come across the mountain board's signs and pilgrim waymarks, usually yellow. One curious thing: we should always follow the arrows uphill, but at some point on the path we will find the same arrows pointing downhill. Ignore them. This happens because the path is also the Camí de Sant Jaume, another pilgrim route that leaves the monastery of Montserrat and joins the Camino Francés, part of the Camino de Santiago. Where people actually go wrong: This route is not difficult. It involves following the path up gentle gradients on obvious ground until you reach the area closest to the monastery. The route suits regular hikers, families, and children used to mountain walking. Terrain, section by section: The toughest part. The first section, from El Pujolet to the Sant Joan turn-off, is the hardest and where most effort is concentrated. You climb about 364 m (1,194 ft) in 3.50 km, so even though it is gentle, pace yourself. The old stone paving. The path still has stretches of old stone paving, though erosion sometimes makes them hard to spot. These stretches mark the old pilgrim way that carried traders and animals up to the monastery. Any exposed sections or scrambling? No. The way is a simple path and asks only for attention, as it is a mountain path with loose stones and uneven ground. There is no water on the path until you reach the monastery, so carry 1 to 1.5 liters per person. At the monastery, there are restrooms and a small supermarket where you can restock whatever you need. This route is almost entirely in the open. Until we get to the monastery area, past the Pla dels Soldats, we will not have any shaded stretches, and by then we will already be very close to the monastery. The mountain has coverage at almost every point along the main paths and plenty of good signage. Download an offline map before you leave. In an emergency, call 112. Take the weather into account whenever you go into the mountains. In summer especially, carry plenty of water, start early, and avoid midday. Visiting Montserrat in each season is a different experience. I recommend enjoying it in spring and fall. If you came to Collbató by bus or car, you will have to get back to Collbató. You have several options: - Walk back, the classic option. - Take a taxi from the monastery. +34 607 237 237 - You can also come off the mountain on the Cremallera de Montserrat (the rack railway) or the cable car, then take a taxi to Collbató. That would be a bonus for getting to know Montserrat. If you want all the information on that option, you can read up here. Either way, this route takes you through the steps of the old pilgrims who came to Montserrat on the Camí de la Costa. You can see with your own eyes and feel in your stride what it was like to cross the heart of this mountain the way the old travelers did, the ones who arrived at the house of Jerusalem, the Marian shrine of Santa Maria de Montserrat, as it says over its entrance: URBS JERUSALEM BEATA DICTA PACIS VISIO ("blessed city of Jerusalem, called the vision of peace").

item.title: United's posh new 'Coastliner' plane is here, set for early 2027 debut
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
After some delays, United Airlines is one step closer to launching service on its posh new domestic plane. The airline on Thursday evening announced it recently took delivery of its first Airbus A321neo “Coastliner” plane. It’s a premium-heavy aircraft that will feature United’s new Polaris business-class suites and a true premium economy cabin. And it will soon be a fixture on the carrier’s top transcontinental routes. United shared a sneak peek of the new jet on social media Thursday evening — well ... the outside of it, at least. This content is hosted by X. As expected, the exterior sports a special wrap featuring the “Coastliner” decal. That’s because United plans to exclusively use this plane on its most premium coast-to-coast flights. Once in service, you’ll see it on routes from Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and San Francisco International Airport (SFO). It will likely also figure into the carrier’s plans at John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), once United makes its long-awaited return to JFK. While United had hoped to launch service on the Coastliner this past summer, delays at Airbus pushed the debut back a few months. The jet is now slated to make its inaugural flight in early 2027, United said this week. It will certainly be an upgrade to the airline’s prime transcontinental service. Seat configuration on United's Airbus A321 Coastliner The aircraft features 10 rows of Polaris suites (20 total) with sliding privacy doors, arranged in a one-by-one configuration. Passengers flying in those suites will get access to United’s Polaris Lounge facilities. There are also 12 Premium Plus recliners across three rows in a two-by-two configuration. Plus, in economy there’s a walk-up snack bar. The whole interior is very similar to the Airbus A321XLR that United debuted late this summer. That longer-range jet is slated to start flying to Europe in the coming months. United’s looming introduction of the Coastliner comes as a growing number of U.S. carriers are upgrading their top transcontinental products. This fall, Alaska Airlines revealed it will add lie-flat suites and premium economy to a future subfleet of Boeing 737 MAX 10 jets. American Airlines last year launched coast-to-coast service with the A321XLR, which sports its latest-generation Flagship Suites up front. Delta Air Lines, meanwhile, rolled out a version of the Airbus A321neo that doesn't have lie-flat seats (at least not yet) but does have a whopping 44 domestic first-class recliners. Plus, JetBlue recently announced that passengers flying in its lie-flat Mint cabins would be entitled to enter its new airport lounges in New York City and Boston, even when flying domestically. United has 50 of these Coastliners (along with 50 of the XLR jets) on order for the coming years. So this aircraft will be a big part of the carrier’s most lucrative domestic service for years to come. Related reading:

item.title: Can Dubai Become the World's Fittest City?
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
At 6 a.m. on Sunday, November 22, Dubai's Sheikh Zayed Road will fall silent. For one morning only, the city's six-lane superhighway—usually a blur of Nissan Patrols, taxis, and delivery scooters—will belong to tens of thousands of competitors as Dubai Run takes over the city’s skyline at dawn, following in the footsteps of a record 307,000 participants last year. Leading the charge is usually Dubai's Crown Prince Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, the driving force behind the Dubai Fitness Challenge (DFC) and one of the city's most ambitious experiments: to turn itself into the fittest city in the world. "The people of Dubai have created an inspirational fitness movement, sending a powerful message that traveled far beyond our city,” Sheikh Hamdan said during a previous edition of the challenge. “Together, let us transform Dubai into the fittest city in the world.” An athlete himself, the Crown Prince has long championed cycling, diving, and long-distance running, but the challenge—now in its tenth year—is his most visible legacy. Launched in 2017, it calls on residents and visitors alike to commit to 30 minutes of exercise every day for 30 days each November. Since its inception, more than 16 million people have taken part, transforming what began as a simple invitation to get moving into one of the world’s largest community fitness initiatives. This year’s landmark edition is running until Sunday, November 29 under the theme What’s Your 30x30?, inviting residents and visitors to find their own way to complete 30 minutes of daily activity. With four flagship events, three free Fitness Villages, and more than 30 Community Fitness Hubs, the program is among the most ambitious yet, transforming everything from beaches and public parks to shopping centers and major roads into places to exercise. Four major events headline the 2026 calendar: Dubai Ride, which opened the challenge on Sunday, November 1 with thousands of cyclists taking over Sheikh Zayed Road; Dubai Run, the world’s largest free community fun run, on Sunday, November 22; Dubai Stand-Up Paddle, a two-day festival of paddle boarding, kayaking and yoga at Hatta Dam on Saturday, November 7 and Sunday, November 8; and Dubai Yoga, which returns for its second edition on Sunday, November 29, bringing thousands together for a mass sunrise session beneath the DIFC Gate Building. Three Fitness Villages—at Kite Beach, Zabeel Park and Al Warqa’a—act as free, all-day wellness hubs offering everything from boxing and beach volleyball to spin classes and meditation. More than 30 neighborhood Community Hubs have also been set up across the city, bringing fitness closer to home with pop-up runs, rooftop yoga, skateboarding lessons, padel tournaments, and family-friendly bootcamps. The calendar aligns with a packed line-up of international sporting events, from the Dubai Premier Padel P1 and T100 Triathlon to the DP World Tour Championship and Emirates Dubai 7s. This year also brings the return of the Dubai Sail Grand Prix, with high-speed catamarans racing off the city’s coastline, while HYROX Dubai will see athletes tackle a grueling combination of running and functional fitness challenges. Elsewhere, the program includes obstacle races, mountain trails in Hatta, and community running events across the city. It’s all part of what His Excellency Saeed Hareb, Secretary General of the Dubai Sports Council, describes as a lasting change in the city’s relationship with exercise. “It has helped establish a culture of active living, bringing communities together and making sport and physical activity an integral part of life in Dubai,” he said as the challenge marked its tenth anniversary. Ahmed Al Khaja, CEO of Dubai Festivals and Retail Establishment, says the anniversary is an opportunity to reflect on how far the initiative has come. Speaking at the launch of the 2026 program, he credited the collaboration between government bodies, private businesses, and local communities with making exercise increasingly accessible across Dubai. The aim, he said, is to inspire healthier habits that continue long after the 30-day challenge ends. The numbers suggest it’s working. Last year’s edition attracted a record three million-plus participants, up from 2.73 million in 2024. More than 307,000 people took part in Dubai Run alone, while Dubai Ride welcomed 40,327 cyclists. Since the challenge launched in 2017, cumulative participation has exceeded 16 million, a remarkable figure for an initiative that began with a simple invitation to exercise for half an hour a day. Ethan Matthews, Chief Operating Officer at Reset Fitness and a former professional rugby player and coach in Portugal and Italy, says that Dubai’s greatest fitness asset is its variety. “There are world-class facilities on every block now—not just gyms, but parks, cycling tracks, and sports complexes,” he says. “Try as many things as possible—team sports, group sessions, individual training. It’s about finding what challenges you physically but also what you actually enjoy. That’s how you stay consistent, especially on the tough days.” For Matthews, the social aspect is just as vital. “The moment you find something you like—padel, CrossFit, running, whatever—you meet people. It opens doors, both personally and professionally. That’s what keeps Dubai’s fitness culture alive.” Anthony Lee, a personal trainer and owner of Activ8 Lifestyle & Fitness who has spent nearly two decades as part of Dubai’s fitness scene, thinks the timing of the challenge is part of its success. “It’s clever,” he says. “It's just before Christmas, when everyone wants to feel a bit fitter before heading home for the holidays, and when the weather’s perfect for being outdoors.” He describes the month-long initiative as “a push that gets people back into routine,” and a rare opportunity to sample new workouts without cost or commitment. “You can try boxing on Kite Beach one day, yoga in Zabeel Park the next. It breaks the monotony.” What stands out most, he adds, is accessibility. “You don’t have to be an athlete. It’s about being a better version of yourself—you versus you.” For visitors, the challenge offers a very different way to experience Dubai as, during November, the city’s hotels, cafes and shopping centers adopt a surprisingly sporty rhythm. At Kite Beach, sunrise yoga sessions fill up fast, while the public running track buzzes with tourists and locals alike, and Zabeel Park hosts evening workouts beneath the skyline. There's no need to sign up—just show up on the day. Outside of November, the spirit of the challenge remains. Dubai has built more than 557 kilometers of cycle tracks, with a goal of 1,000 kilometers by 2030, and the urban planning department is adding shaded walking routes to make exercise feasible for longer stretches of the year. Lee, the personal trainer, believes Dubai’s fitness drive has found fertile ground because of the city’s demographic and design. “It’s a young place,” he says. “Most people are working-age expats, and with the beach and pool culture here, people want to look and feel good.” But vanity isn’t the whole story. “Every new residential tower has a gym and a pool, so exercise is built into daily life,” he says. “When I moved here 18 years ago, you had a handful of hotel gyms and a couple of Fitness First branches. Now every neighborhood has options, from boutique studios to outdoor circuits.” He has also noticed a social shift: “Fitness has become a way to meet people. For newcomers, joining a class or trying padel is how you find your tribe.” The fitness calendar's cleverest invention, however, might be the Mallathon. With summer temperatures soaring past 45°C, nine of the city’s biggest malls were converted into indoor running routes between June and September, attracting 100,000 participants. Dr Amir Firouzjaei, a general practitioner and traditional Chinese medicine expert who has lived in Dubai for three years, believes the movement taps into something deeper. “When a city moves, its energy moves,” he says. “It’s not only about training the body but refreshing the mind and spirit.” He explains that the city’s blend of high-intensity exercise and restorative practices “keeps the balance between energy and recovery,” preventing burnout and encouraging people to “stick with it.” The trend is filtering into Dubai's hospitality scene, too. New-generation hotels such as SIRO One Za’abeel pitch themselves as “fitness and recovery” spaces, complete with in-room stretching areas, altitude chambers and performance coaches. In Al Quoz, the Matcha Club—a blend of padel courts, co-working space, and cafe—has become the new social hang-out for the health-minded. Even Dubai’s famously indulgent brunches are getting lighter, with restaurants like Eat Well dishing up bowls, turmeric shots, and cold-brew coffee instead of the traditional Champagne towers. Matthews, who moved to Dubai in 2017—the same year the first Dubai Fitness Challenge launched—says he’s watched the city’s attitudes shift dramatically. “Post-Covid, the appetite for fitness just exploded,” he says. “Gyms, studios and open-air facilities have multiplied, but more importantly, people’s reasons for exercising have changed. They’re doing it to feel good, not just to look good.” He believes that’s partly because of education and access. “The government has played a big role through campaigns like 30x30, but accessibility is the real game changer. Whether it’s walking paths, beach gyms or purpose-built cycling tracks, there’s always somewhere to move.” For Matthews, that accessibility underpins a healthy, sustainable economy. “When people feel better, they perform better—at work, at home, everywhere. Fitness has become part of Dubai.” Firouzjaei, the doctor, sees Dubai’s fitness boom as part of a wider cultural shift. “It’s a fast city, and that creates pressure,” he says. “People here work hard and compete hard, so they need ways to recharge and reset.” He points out that the city’s international mix has made wellness more mainstream. “Residents come from everywhere—Asia, Europe, the Middle East—and many already know yoga, acupuncture, or functional medicine,” he says. “They’re open to new ideas and they understand that health is an investment rather than a luxury.” In his clinic, he’s noticed that even patients who once focused purely on appearance now talk about sleep, stress, and balance. Behind the lifestyle messaging lies the emirate's urban agenda. Dubai wants to be a ‘20-minute city,’ where every resident can reach work, shops, and recreation within a short cycle or walk. The health argument is compelling. Obesity and diabetes are major public health concerns across the Gulf, and studies show only one in five UAE children meets recommended daily activity levels. City officials believe that building infrastructure—parks, cycle paths, open gyms—is the surest way to shift behavior. Already, habits are changing. Park footfall has risen 20% year-on-year, while corporate wellness participation has grown by 30%. The once-novel sight of commuters jogging to metro stations has become almost ordinary. For tourists, taking part couldn’t be easier. The Dubai Fitness Challenge app lists daily events, classes, and pop-ups across the city, most of them free. Looking back on 18 years in Dubai, Lee says the transformation has been “massive.” When he first arrived, “there were far fewer gyms, and fitness wasn’t part of daily conversation.” Now, he says, it’s as visible as the skyline itself. “Sure, some people join the big events just for the photos—you’ll always have that—but for others it’s the start of something lasting,” he says. “Even if they only do the challenge for a month, it plants a seed. And that’s what counts.” Matthews agrees, though he cautions against seeing Dubai’s fitness scene as something reserved for the elite. “The biggest misconception is that you have to be in peak shape to take part,” he says. “You don’t. Fitness here is for everyone, from people training for Ironman to those who just want to walk their dogs or join a weekend bootcamp.” Dubai has always been a city in motion, but now it wants its progress measured not by the height of its towers or the size of its megaprojects, but by footsteps, pedal strokes and heartbeats. It's a city that’s, quite literally, on the move—and inviting the world to keep up. Five fun things to do during Dubai Fitness Challenge 2026 1. Run among Dubai’s gleaming skyscrapers Dubai’s biggest community running event transforms Sheikh Zayed Road into a traffic-free running track, with participants choosing between a 5km route through Downtown Dubai or a longer 10km course finishing beneath the DIFC Gate Building. More than 307,000 runners took part last year. Where: Sheikh Zayed Road, starting near the Museum of the Future When: Sunday, November 22, 6.30 a.m. How to take part: Register free at at dubaifitnesschallenge.com. Marking the finale of Dubai Fitness Challenge, thousands of yoga enthusiasts will gather beneath the iconic DIFC Gate Building for a mass sunrise session. The program includes guided breathwork, a sound bath and a 30-minute yoga session, with dedicated areas for families and women. Dubai’s largest beachfront Fitness Village returns with everything from spinning and yoga to padel, beach volleyball, basketball and cricket. There are dedicated activity zones, bookable courts and daily fitness classes, with the Arabian Gulf providing a rather spectacular backdrop. When: Saturday, October 31 to Sunday, November 29; weekdays 3 p.m.–11 p.m., weekends 7 a.m.–11 p.m. How to take part: Register free on-site, with selected activities available to book at dubaifitnesschallenge.com. Zabeel Park’s Fitness Village returns with boxing, spinning, basketball, padel, and daily group workouts, alongside dedicated children’s activities. The village also serves as the official bib collection point for Dubai Run. When: Saturday, October 31 to Sunday, November 29; weekdays 4 p.m.–11 p.m., weekends noon–11 p.m. Set among palm trees and parkland, this neighborhood-style Fitness Village combines outdoor exercise with family-friendly activities. There’s a 2.8km running and cycling track, bike rentals, daily fitness classes, dedicated ladies-only areas and courts for padel, volleyball, football, and basketball. When: Saturday, October 31 to Sunday, November 29; daily 4 p.m.–11 p.m. This article was originally published on Condé Nast Traveller Middle East.

item.title: REVIEW: My favourite countryside homestay: a slick and stylish multi-gen home with private tennis courts and a heated swimming pool
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
October is a month of birthdays in our family and this year was an especially momentous one. Two key players had fortieth and a sixteenth celebrations two days apart and, as if by magic, both landed over a weekend. A family staycation was the obvious answer; finding somewhere that worked for us all was less easy to conjure up. There were 12 of us in total, with ages spanning an impressive 73 years. Needless to say, our interests are varied, but it was neither the oldest or the youngest that proved trickiest to please. Teenagers are a breed of their own and I’m inexperienced when it comes to providing entertainment for anyone over the age of four. But as there were three secondary school-age kids in our group, one being the reason we were celebrating in the first place, finding somewhere they’d love was paramount. In my role at Condé Nast Traveller, I’m lucky enough to browse and lust over beautiful hotels, Airbnbs and private homes for most of the working day, and I’ve got a wishlist as long as my arm for adults-only escapes and places I’m longing to take my smalls. It was useless: this particular assignment meant starting a whole new search. Enter Unique Homestays and Redmere Hall, the 22-bed ground-floor home in the heart of the Wiltshire countryside. Once a stable with a history dating back to 1838, it’s been beautifully restored to host groups exactly like ours and it couldn’t have been more perfect. The magpie in me was drawn to the aesthetic, curated by London-based branding and interiors agency Run for the Hills, whose masterful eye for design referenced the building’s equestrian heritage in a way that felt spot-on for the modern family. The kitchen was especially ‘wow’ with an enormous wooden table, three ovens, enough glasses to fuel two nights of eating and drinking and a traditional stable door leading into the garden. Outside, tennis courts, a heated swimming pool, a cedar hot tub and an impressive stone barbecue meant we had zero reason to leave, and no-one had the chance to feel bored. That in itself was a deal-cincher, but then I spotted the most fun room in the house – the eight-person bunk room with its deep-red wooden beds and direct access to the pool. This was where the younger members of our group spent most of their evenings, cosying up playing games and reading on the top bunks, tucking their toys into the lower beds and really making themselves at home. Meanwhile, the rest of us lost ourselves in the maze of living spaces, from the dining room with its bespoke 20-person table to the impeccably designed lounge (I felt like I’d stepped into my own private Soho House) and cinema room with its C-shaped sofa and mega-stylish Bang and Olufsen sound bar. We spent the weekend exactly as you’d imagine, dipping in and out of the pool or hot tub, spotting peacocks in the grounds and combining our efforts to cook, mix, pour and serve course after course of family favourites. Every now and then, someone would take the short drive into Frome, the artsy neighbouring town, and return with quirky souvenirs or goodies from the local farm shop. Other than that we were completely equipped with everything we might need. Uninterrupted time together was the aim, and Redmere Hall made it possible to please the masses equally. It set the bar for a wonderful multi-generational staycation and the house itself ended up being the base for one of the year’s best weekends. For a special occasion, I’m sure I’d find nowhere better.

item.title: Albania’s restored stone houses throw open the doors to visitors
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel
Sunlight pours through a tiny stone window, causing the wooden floorboards to creak as they warm up. The sound of sheep’s bells filters in from a passing flock. The scent of baking bread mingles with smoke from the previous evening’s fire. I wake up feeling I’ve been transported back to another time – but in reality I’m in modern-day Albania. I’m staying in a kulla, one of the traditional stone tower houses that are found throughout northern Albania, Montenegro and North Macedonia. They once protected families during times of conflict and sheltered weary travellers on trade routes, before mostly falling into disrepair in the 20th century. A new long-distance trail developed by the Albanian Agritourism Association aims to return some of them to their former glory and give visitors a chance to discover a part of Albania almost untouched by tourism. The Tower Trail passes through some of the least visited areas of north-eastern Albania, with stops in the Mirdita, Mat, Bulqiza and Dibra regions. Designed to be walked with a guide over nine days, the journey spans more than 100 miles through traditional villages, high plains, forests and river valleys, with future plans for cycling and 4x4 routes. Some stages of the trail are long, and can easily be broken up into two days, or shortened with a car transfer. Opportunities to stay in guesthouses, farms and kullas help connect travellers with the cultural heritage of the region, in a way that is becoming increasingly difficult in more popular parts of the country. The kulla, in its many forms, is the central feature of the trail. Traditionally constructed from limestone and wood from the surrounding mountains, kullas follow a regular architectural structure, but also represent the character of the families who commissioned them. Built by highly skilled craftsmen, early versions were made to withstand the region’s harsh weather conditions and even harsher historical realities, including the 15th-century Ottoman invasion and frequent tribal disputes. Many more were built in the 18th and 19th centuries, but under Albania’s communist regime, from 1944 until 1991, many families had their kullas confiscated, only to find them in disrepair when they reclaimed them. Today, many sit empty after a mass exodus from rural Albania to the cities in the 1990s and 2000s. “We are losing traditions because people aren’t staying here,” Nik Nikolli tells me as we walk through the hilltop village of Lufaj on the trail’s first stage. Nikolli is the director of Infokulla, a small museum and cultural centre in the nearby town of Rubik, which provides free hiking maps and historical information about the region. He explains that many of the villages along the route have just one or two families remaining. Introducing the idea of tourism has been slow because the concept of accepting money from a guest goes against highly established traditions of hospitality. He hopes the trail will encourage local people to open their kullas or farms as guesthouses, providing unique experiences to visitors while earning a bit of extra income for their families. Walking the trail, it’s easy to see what Nikolli means about the lack of people in the villages and the hospitality of those who remain. On several days, our journey takes longer than expected as my guide and I are regularly invited to sit for a coffee and served a bounty of freshly harvested grapes, plums and walnuts. Agriculture is the mainstay of life in these areas, and people are hard at work in the fields from dawn until dusk. Yet they always seem eager to take a break, entertain visitors and share tales from the past. Much of the Tower Trail is centred on old roads through hilly karst terrain dotted with caves, chestnut trees and cornfields. Trail markings are still sporadic and some bushwhacking is required, but the route allows travellers to walk the paths still used by villagers today, with plenty of opportunities for interactions. At the end of my second day on the trail, in the village of Derjan, 91-year-old Hajrija Qerimi is beaming as she tells me about growing up in a large kulla nearby. Her father was a successful farmer, still remembered for his generosity, and the family regularly hosted travellers. She tells me there were never fewer than 10 people at the dinner table. “My father advised me early on that everyone who comes to the house is offered food and drink, and he taught me what and how to serve,” she says, proudly. “The important thing was that nobody left without receiving the absolute best hospitality.” One of the highlights of the trail is the chance for travellers to experience that traditional hospitality while staying in restored kullas. On day four, in the hillside village of Dushaj, I stay at Kulla Hupi, which opened as a guesthouse in 2021. The owner, Luli Hupi, spent years working in a nearby mine, saving to restore the house room by room. “When you come here, there’s a family waiting for you, and you feel you’re at home,” he says. Running more than just a business venture, Hupi is keen to support the local community. He works with more than 10 families who provide all of the restaurant’s meat, cheese, honey, bread and other produce, while also serving as guides for hiking, horseback riding excursions and cooking classes. He keeps his guest numbers low, and has no interest in the trend towards mass tourism in Albania. “People say I’m stupid for not having 50 tables at the restaurant,” he laughs, as we sit next to a roaring fire in the oda, the traditional sitting room, after a simple dinner of warm corn bread, fig jam, pickled salads, goat’s cheese and gjizë, a type of cottage cheese. “But I don’t want 50 tables, I want 10, and I want people to have to reserve a month in advance.” Hupi’s influence can clearly be felt in the surrounding area, where many kullas are undergoing restoration, and the idea of a slower form of tourism is being embraced. On my penultimate night, I stay at Butterfly Camping, a small site situated in a canyon on the banks of the Black Drin River. The owner, Labinot Murrja, lights an open fire, pours me a glass of local grape brandy, and tells me how he and his father cleared and levelled the land along the riverbank themselves. They kept things simple, building three small cabins, leaving room to erect some tents, tables and a shed with a basic kitchen. Murrja says he’s not interested in casting a wide net for tourists, but is targeting people with an adventurous side, an interest in nature and a desire to experience life in the nearby village, where he still lives with his family. He tells me local people were sceptical when he started, wondering why anyone would have an interest in coming to the middle of nowhere. Yet when they saw guests arrive, they were convinced, and Murrja says similar businesses are now popping up in the wider region. Like Hupi, Murrja emphasises that he’s interested in providing a unique experience for visitors, rather than making a big profit. “I love this job,” he says with a grin. “It doesn’t make you rich, I’m just doing it for passion.” Albania’s tourism industry has been booming in recent years. However, ongoing protests, sparked by the planned construction of a luxury resort in a protected coastal area, have seen locals voice their frustration at the pace and unsustainable nature of development in the country. With so much of Albania’s tourism concentrated on the coast and northern Alps, rural inland areas have been left struggling to find what they have to offer visitors. In embracing the kulla and their strong tradition of hospitality, they may just have found it. The trip was supported by Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ). For more information, visit the Albanian Agritourism Association. A double room in a kulla costs from about £35 a night

item.title: IDEA: 53 Healthy Thanksgiving Recipes to Brighten Up the Table
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
What makes a healthy Thanksgiving recipe? To us, it’s less about cutting out butter or skipping pie and more about bringing balance to the table. Crisp, bitter greens make creamy mashed potatoes taste even better. Tart cranberries cut through rich turkey gravy. Beans, whole grains, and plenty of colorful vegetables bring flavor, texture, and variety to a meal that can otherwise skew decidedly beige. These healthy Thanksgiving recipes cover the entire feast, from crunchy salads and make-ahead appetizers to satisfying plant-forward mains and festive desserts. Some offer more fiber or protein; others give seasonal produce a starring role. What they have in common is that every one is delicious. You’ll also find plenty of vegan, gluten-free, and dairy-free options too. Because there’s room for everyone—and everything—at the Thanksgiving table.

item.title: How to Watch the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
As the turkey thaws and a day of cooking prep begins, an equally integral Thanksgiving tradition is Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. Last year, 3.5 million spectators lined New York City’s streets to watch the procession of vibrant balloons and whimsical floats bob and weave through Midtown Manhattan to the beats of countless marching bands and celebrity performers. Beyond the city, a record-setting 34.3 million tuned into the NBC and Peacock broadcast, making the Emmy-winning production the year’s most-watched entertainment telecast. This year's promises to be even grander, as 2026 marks the 100th anniversary of the spectacle, which started in 1924 (though it wasn’t held from 1942 to 1944 because parade materials were reserved for wartime efforts). “As a kid from the Bronx, it is an honor to bring this cherished tradition…to the city of New York every year,” the parade’s executive producer since 2021 Will Coss tells Condé Nast Traveler. The annual highlight for him is seeing the joyful expressions of spectators of all ages as the parade passes them by “showcasing some of the most iconic and recognizable pop culture characters and figures.” On the eve of the parade's centennial, the team—composed of painters, carpenters, animators, sculptures, welders, designers, engineers, and electricians—is honoring its past by way of revived classics like Felix the Cat and Underdog balloons. Ardent fans will also find a swath of newcomers that include a Fantasia-inspired Mickey, cowboy Minion, and a Peanuts duo. “The team at Macy’s Studios works year-round to make this historic parade bigger and better for our audiences every year,” Coss says. Here’s everything you need to know about the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in 2026—all its surprises, delights, and familiar joys. How did the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade start? When Macy’s first debuted its one-million-square foot New York City flagship store at 34th Street between Broadway and Seventh Avenues in 1924, the retailer threw a Christmas parade on Thanksgiving morning to boost holiday sales—with a much longer route starting at 145 Street and Covent Avenue. Balloons joined the lineup in 1927, starting with Felix the Cat, and the festivities were first broadcast nationally in 1947. What is the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade’s route now? These days, the festive parade follows a 2.5-mile path from the Upper East Side to Midtown Manhattan. Starting at the corner of 77th Street and Central Park West, the route heads south to Columbus Circle and then turns east, heading along 59th Street to Sixth Avenue. From there, it goes straight down Sixth Avenue to 34th Street, ending in front of Macy’s flagship store in Herald Square. What’s the best way to see the parade in person? Coss recommends arriving early for a great view. Many spectators start to gather as early as 6 a.m. along the beginning of the route on Central Park West (approach from the west) from 61st to 75th Streets. Other prime spots include the south side of 59th Street between Columbus Circle and Sixth Avenue and the entire stretch of Sixth Avenue between 38th and 59th. Spectators should be aware there is no viewing on Central Park West between 59th and 60th Streets, or anywhere south of 38th Street. Coss also reminds those bringing children to dress warmly for the chilly weather and to be prepared to entertain young ones for a few hours while waiting to spot the first float. He suggests avoiding strollers, large bags, backpacks, and umbrellas. What’s on the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade 2026 lineup? In celebration of its centennial, some 100 inflatables will fly. Returning after decades are much-anticipated Felix the Cat (the parade's first character balloon, introduced in 1927) and Blue Hippopotamus (from the 1931 parade), while Hello Kitty and Underdog (who appeared in every parade from 1965 through 1984) will also make cameos. New to the scene are Bluey, Buckaroo Bob the Minion, and Snoopy persona Joe Cool with Woodstock, among others. The procession will also welcome 52 floats, 31 clown crews, nine specialty units (such as trycaloons, or balloons ridden on tricycles), seven marching bands, and five balloonicles (that’s a balloon-vehicle hybrid). TODAY’s Savannah Guthrie, Hoda Kotb, and Al Roker will host the live broadcast of the 100th Macy’s Parade. Though this year's performance lineup has yet to be announced, the 2025 roster featured 26 celebrity performers, ranging from Colbie Caillat and Christopher Jackson to Foreigner and Taylor Momsen, complete with a performance by KPop Demon Hunters’ HUNTR/X singing voices EJAE, Audrey Nuna, and Rei Ami. As anticipation for the parade's centennial only increases, Coss says this year will “bring new surprises and delights to the iconic holiday tradition and truly celebrate this incredibly special anniversary.” How can I watch the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade on TV? Americans can watch the live telecast on both NBC and Peacock on Thursday, November 26, from 8:30 a.m. to noon in all time zones, while Telemundo will air a Spanish-language simulcast hosted by Andrea Meza, Aleyda Ortiz, and Clovis Nienow. For late risers, an encore will air starting at 2 p.m. ET/PT, and the full broadcast will also be on NBC with live audio description on Secondary Audio Program channel (SAP). Behind-the-scenes footage will be shared on social media @macys and #MacysParade via Instagram, TikTok, and Threads. To rev up for the turkey day excitement, “Countdown to the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade” will air on Wednesday, November 25, on NBC and Peacock. The primetime special will broadcast live from the parade starting line with exclusive previews and behind-the-scenes stories from the balloons and floats. How else can I experience the Thanksgiving Day Parade excitement? One of the most underrated—and free—ways to experience the parade is by attending the Thanksgiving Eve balloon inflating event on Wednesday, November 25, a “time-honored tradition and special peek into the parade celebrations,” Coss says. Since 1994, the Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade has invited guests to see the process the balloons undergo to reach their larger-than-life size and scale the afternoon before Thanksgiving. Last year’s took place between 1 p.m. and 6 p.m., with the line opening at noon. Those interested can enter at West 72nd Street and Columbus Avenue, where they’ll be guided through a security checkpoint and then can roam between West 77th and 81st Streets to view the balloons. Note that prohibited items include bags or backpacks larger than 12-by-6-by-12 inches, lawn chairs, large coolers, alcoholic beverages, chairs, weapons, drones, pets, and umbrellas; participants will be screened before entering the route. Where can I get more information on the Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade? For the latest up-to-date information, visit macys.com/parade for details on the parade and nbc.com/macys-thanksgiving-day-parade for updates on the broadcast.

item.title: Silversea unveils the southernmost hotel in the world, purpose-built for Antarctica trips
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
There’s now a new reason to travel to the bottom of the world. Silversea on Thursday officially opened The Cormorant at 55 South, a new luxury hotel near the southern tip of South America designed to transform the experience of traveling to Antarctica. Located in Chile's Patagonia region near Puerto Williams, the world's southernmost settlement, the 150-room property will serve as a luxury base and launch pad for Silversea's high-end fly-cruise trips to Antarctica — journeys that begin with a flight from Puerto Williams to a research station at Antarctica's King George Island. Once there, travelers board a Silversea expedition ship to explore Antarctica. “Silversea has always been about going further, and for our guests heading to Antarctica, that journey now begins here at the southernmost hotel on Earth, with the kind of welcome they’ve come to expect from us,” Silversea president Bert Hernandez said during an unveiling event at the hotel. TPG is one of just a handful of travel media outlets getting an early look at the property this week. Until now, Silversea's fly-cruise passengers have stayed in non-Silversea hotels in Punta Arenas, Chile ahead of a charter flight to King George Island. The less-than-ideal arrangement meant guests were booked across various hotels, while the line was left scrambling for additional rooms whenever bad weather delayed or grounded flights to Antarctica. Now, with The Cormorant at 55 South, guests can relax in modern luxury overnight — or sit out bad weather — just minutes from their charter flight. Better yet, the expedition begins well before they step aboard their ship. While at the hotel, guests will be able to try on or swap their Silversea-provided Antarctica polar gear, complete biosecurity checks that are necessary before visiting the continent, and clean any personal equipment they plan to take ashore, as well as attend an initial Antarctica briefing — activities that usually take place on the ship. They'll also get a chance to explore Patagonia’s breathtaking wilderness on guided excursions around the hotel, including kayaking, hiking, birdwatching and horseback riding. A shuttle bus will also take guests into Puerto Williams. “The idea was that this wasn’t a stopover hotel. This is the first and last impression that we make on our guests, and so we wanted that to be memorable,” Hernandez said at a press conference ahead of an official ribbon-cutting ceremony. What to expect at the southernmost hotel on earth Initially conceived in 2018 as a turnaround hub for Antarctica, the Cormorant at 55 South has become a destination that by Hernandez’s own admission is “more beautiful than anyone ever envisioned." Designed to blend in with the environment, the low-slung hotel features soaring ceilings, concrete floors, natural wood, stone and earthy textiles punctuated by pops of orange, yellow and green — colours that echo the surrounding terrain. Floor-to-ceiling glass means the view is never far away, be it forest, sea or snow-scratched mountains, stretching from the jagged peaks of Dientes de Navarino to the Andes in Argentina. “It was always incredibly important that the hotel reflect the environment,” Silversea senior vice president of expeditions Conrad Combrink said during unveiling events. Elements of fire and ice inform the design, alongside the darkness of the Drake Passage and the Beagle Channel, just beyond the hotel. Being in the “land of fire”, the hotel fittingly has a massive indoor firepit, surrounded by lounges and easy chairs. An outside terrace offers more places to sit and take in the scenery. Rooms are simply designed, with a view of mountain or sea, and pair a soothing mix of local wood, natural textiles and green upholstery. There’s a Nespresso machine and a small bar fridge with water and craft beer from a brewery in Punta Arenas. Latitude 55, the onsite restaurant, showcases regional flavors, including excellent empanadas and a stand-out asado barbecue served on the first night of any stay, slow-cooked over an open fire in the hotel grounds.. At Bar Sur, guests can sample Chilean wine, enjoy a pisco sour tasting or try a cocktail made with calafete, a berry indigenous to Puerto Williams. The Uncharted Boutique is the place to stock up on beautifully made Chilean handicrafts or last-minute polar gear. More than a hotel stay, The Cormorant at 55 South marks a wider shift for Silversea,which will now base all its Antarctica expeditions out of Puerto Williams. Previously only sailings that crossed the Drake Passage left from Puerto Williams. While most Antarctic operators base their fleets out of Ushuaia, Argentina, Silversea is the only cruise line running operations out of Puerto Williams. Located further south along the Beagle Channel, Puerto Williams provides a shorter, more direct launch point into the Drake Passage. Silversea's fly-cruise trips allow Antarctica-bound travelers to skip a ship-based voyage across the Drake Passage — the notoriously rough, 600-mile-wide waterway separating the tip of South America and Antarctica. Guests fly from Santiago directly to Puerto Williams for an overnight stay at The Cormorant, before taking a charter flight across the Drake to King George Island in Antarctica's South Shetland Islands, where their expedition ship awaits. Upon return, guests spend another night at the hotel before flying back to Santiago. The opening of the Cormorant at 55 South coincides with Silversea's largest Antarctic season to date. Fly-cruise itineraries now dominate the line’s offerings in Antarctica, accounting for 29 of its 40 total sailings across three expedition vessels: Silver Endeavour, Silver Wind, and Silver Cloud. The hotel will currently stay open from October through March, but there is talk it will open year-round, for travelers to southern Chile looking for a soft landing after adventures. More than a place to stay, The Cormorant makes the journey south feel like an experience in its own right — a fittingly rugged starting point for what lies ahead, plus unique bragging rights of having stayed at the southernmost hotel on earth.
