item.title: IDEA: Finland Is Throwing an Epic Dinner Party for 16 Singles—Here's How to Get Invited
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
The Nordic countries are well known for their rather gimmicky yet innovative travel campaigns luring travelers to the icy north. From doctors prescribing travel to Sweden as a medical treatment to Oslo's viral mock-documentary narrated by a jaded local called Halfdan. Preceding these by a decade, Danish tour operator Spies Travels famously promoted its ”Do It for Denmark!” campaign focused on Denmark’s low birth rates, offering “ovulation discounts” to couples who proved they conceived on their romantic trip. Now, Finland has announced it's flying out sixteen international singles this February for a "blind group date with likeminded travelers and local Finnish singles.” The country is touting the so-called Love At First Bite campaign as an epic blind dinner date, designed to help participants “discover Finnish food, meet new people, and perhaps even find love.” The singles will be divided and hosted in two group dates in capital city Helsinki and Tampere located in Europe’s largest lake district, Finland’s Lakeland region. Joining the singles over candlelit tasting menus crafted by local celebrity chefs will be local single Finns. Get ready for lots of prolonged eye contact—the Nordic way of flirting—under low light as you bond over the likes of wild trout, reindeer, chanterelle mushrooms, and sea buckthorn. For those heading to Tampere, the destination is monikered the “world’s sauna capital,” so chances of sweating with your fellow single strangers is probably on the menu too. I’ll admit, when the campaign was launched worldwide, my Finnish friends and I wrinkled our noses in confusion. Romantic and sexy aren’t the first words that come to mind when you think of Finland. And it's not the Nordic country you'd first go to for love if we're talking stereotypes. The Danes have their extroverted charm, the Swedes their chic worldliness, and the Norwegians typically have more money to spend on you. Popular Nordic comedians Helgi and Erlend riff on these regional stereotypes, depicting their Finnish character as stoic, quiet and mentally tough. The very Finnish ethos of “sisu” means grit and the tenacity to push through tough times. But maybe those are qualities you'd want in a lifelong partner as you navigate challenges together. So the campaign got me thinking a little deeper. Named the happiest country in the world for the ninth consecutive year in a row, Finns are satisfied with their lifestyles firmly rooted in the outdoors, nature, and a slower pace of life. In this contentment is where you’ll find Finland’s hidden sexier side. In a country of roughly five million, there are two million saunas. And few places are more intimate than sweating together naked in a sauna, dipping in chilly lakes during winter, then warming back up indoors in many more ways. There’s also something rather romantic about grilling wild-caught salmon for two over an open flame in the backcountry. This isn’t the first time the country has dabbled in an unconventional approach to dating. The viral “Sinkkukori” phenomenon introduced pink shopping baskets as a way for singles to covertly signal their availability. Now Finland is taking a more overt approach to romance. As the well-known nineteenth-century English idiom reminds us, the quickest way to the heart is through the stomach, and Finland certainly wants to put this to the test. To shoot your shot at finding love in Finland, apply by November 10, 2026 at 11:59 AM Finnish time. All you have to do is make a video answering the question: what would you serve on a dinner date, and why? Just like a proper prospect, Finland would like to know your preferences in advance so it can woo you in the most epic and intentional way. If that isn’t romantic, I don’t know what is. This article was originally published on Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: American Airlines business class to Prague for just 55,000 points: Here's how you can do it, too
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
American Airlines business class to Prague for just 55,000 points: Here's how you can do it, too It's not often that you can fly from the U.S. to Europe in business class for just 55,000 points, but sometimes, deals are out there — especially if you use American Airlines AAdvantage miles or Atmos Rewards points. I found a great award using Atmos Rewards Points on American Airlines' newly resumed nonstop flight from Philadelphia to Prague. As mentioned, I paid just 55,000 points (and $5.60 in taxes and fees). I'll get into some detail on how to find these kinds of deals, but first, let's talk a bit more about this flight. I wanted the chance to check American's European service and compare the business-class products on the older 787-8s (like the one I flew to Prague) and the new premium-heavy 787-9P planes I've flown to London. American Airlines relaunched its Prague service in May of this year. It had previously served the route for a few years, in 2018 and 2019, before abandoning it during the coronavirus pandemic. AA now operates the route seasonally during the busy summer period, from May to October, between Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) and Václav Havel Airport Prague (PRG). The airline has already said the route will return for summer 2027. Another good sign for the route: AA is adding more European destinations from Philadelphia next summer, including Vienna and Porto, Portugal. American Airlines calls Prague part of "the airline's Central European network." I kicked off my journey with a few days in Philadelphia before heading to the airport. American Airlines Flagship Lounge Philadelphia American Airlines' Flagship Lounge at Philadelphia opened in May of last year, after years of delays. It is a lovely space to spend a few hours before your flight, though it can get crowded at times. I could access it because I was flying long-haul business class. A great American Airlines agent named Thomas Doersam, who has been with AA for 38 years, gave me a quick tour of the Flagship and the adjacent Admirals Club. The Flagship lounge (American's fifth) is near Gate A15, where AA's long-haul flights depart. Eligible passengers flying long-haul business class can use the Flagship Lounge, which includes those in business class on these flights. Others have access to the Admiral's Club just across the way. It has been lovely to see American Airlines invest so much in its lounge product. In fact, a sixth Flagship lounge was announced for Charlotte, along with a massive new Admiral's Club that will clock in at more than 40,000 square feet. I had seat 1L on this 11-year-old Boeing 787 Dreamliner, with the ship number N806AA. This is a legacy interior that will eventually be phased out. TPG reported that these planes will receive new Flagship business-class suites and a full cabin refresh, though AA didn't say when that would start. I was on the smallest Dreamliner variant, and the business-class cabin had just 20 seats in a 1-2-1 configuration. All the seats had aisle access. These lie-flat seats were 21 inches wide and featured American's version of the Safran Concept D seat (formerly known as Zodiac). I found them to be fairly comfortable, if a bit narrow, during the overnight journey. Some flyers complain about these seats since some are rear-facing. The seats are attached to each other, and some people say they feel it when the person seated next to them moves. (Some flyers even refer to them as "rocking chairs.") It never bothered me on my previous trips in these seats, and it didn't this time either, even though I was in the first row. There were also 28 premium economy seats on this plane — a comfortable and potentially more affordable option. There were also 186 economy seats, including 48 Main Cabin Extra seats. Inflight entertainment was provided by a 15-inch screen that could pop out with the push of a button. There were plenty of shows and movies to choose from. Still, these screens are showing their age, especially now that more innovative 4K screens are rolling out across many fleets (including American's). Inflight Wi-Fi was provided by Panasonic and cost $35 for the full flight. It was just OK, and I was glad I wasn't relying on it for important work. American Airlines will begin rolling out Starlink Wi-Fi in 2027, but in the meantime, representatives say there are plans to improve Wi-Fi speeds on its 787s, too. I expect the overall tech picture to improve dramatically over the next few years. The airlines have had some pretty major connection problems recently. Remember, these seats are a decade old and show a bit of wear and tear. Still, it's a comfortable cabin, and because there are so few business-class seats, it does feel a bit special. My seat had plenty of other bells and whistles that I won't go into too much detail here, but I appreciated the overhead air vents and some of the nooks and crannies for storing items. I also loved American's newer bedding. The zipper bag held a large blanket and pillow; mattress pads were also available at each seat. While it may not look as fancy as United's Saks bedding, I found it super comfortable. Amenity kits were made in honor of the World Cup, featuring a clear design filled with standard amenities. You can read more details about the hard product on these planes in the reviews linked above, but I think, in general, I'm a bigger fan than most when it comes to the seats on these Dreamliners. Comparing the new premium 787Ps and the older 787-8s As I mentioned, I don't mind the older 787s, but there's no question: American's new 787Ps are a fresher product. TPG's Eric Rosen and I reviewed the new product last year, and we were both pretty impressed. AA unveiled its all-new Flagship Suite business class in May, and Eric and I were eager to experience the new planes and try out the Flagship Suite Preferred and Flagship Suite business-class seats. He took a flight from London to Chicago, and I was flying from Chicago to London. Unlike the 787-8s, which have just 20 business-class seats, the new 787Ps have a whopping 51 Flagship Suites. It will be interesting to see whether AA expands the business-class and premium-class cabins during the retrofit of these planes. You can really see the differences in the photos below. Aside from the size of the business-class cabin, the biggest difference is the sliding doors on the 787Ps. But there are other differences, too. There are eight Flagship Suite Preferred seats on the 787Ps — an upgraded version of the new suites with additional space. Finally, the new 787Ps have updated designs, more storage, a lounger mode on the seat controls, wireless charging and dramatically better 17.3-inch IFE screens with both Bluetooth and touchscreen capability. While I love the new planes, I wouldn't choose a more expensive redemption just to fly them. I had a great crew on my flight to Prague, with friendly service and generally good food and beverage. Not only did we get a predeparture beverage, but service was prompt, friendly and efficient. Dinner started with warmed nuts and a beverage of your choice. Appetizers included a small romaine salad, along with citrus-poached shrimp and ceviche-style fish. For a main course, I finally tried American Airlines' new "sliders and fries." It was only available as a pre-order, but I'm so glad I took the time to select it because it was delicious. Dessert was the classic sundae which I ordered with extra whipped cream. How can you resist? Breakfast was yogurt with granola and fruit that AA calls a "fresh fruit bowl" — perfectly fine for an airplane breakfast. The best part was the multiple cappuccinos I drank. (American brought back espresso drinks in business class in 2025, and I've made full use of the perk.) There were also snacks set up midflight. I even received a thank-you note from my flight attendant, Daniel — a rare and lovely touch that I don't often find with U.S. airlines. As I mentioned, I scored my business-class seat for just 55,000 Atmos Rewards points and $5.60 in taxes and fees. Remember, you can book American Airlines flights using Alaska points, and it can often be an even better deal. Often, when a new route is launched or resumed, you'll see airlines make award tickets more available than usual. That's just what happened here, when the airline made business-class redemptions on both Prague and its newly resumed Budapest route widely available, even on partners like Alaska. When a new route starts or an old one resumes, check award availability as soon as the seats go on sale. Other hacks to score hard-to-find redemptions To start, flexibility is key. If you can be flexible on dates and destinations, the world literally opens up. Let the deal guide where you go. Try booking as soon as schedules open up. For carriers like Japan Airlines, you'll find the best availability 11 months in advance, as that's when seats open to partner airlines. Award search tools have also become a huge part of my process. Seats.aero, ExpertFlyer (owned by TPG parent company, Red Ventures) and Roame.travel are my favorites. I also love the award tool Points Path, which sits on my browser, so I see award availability when I search on Google Flights. American Airlines also has a great tool that I use to find deals. I use the airline's award search calendar to find business-class seats for months at a time. Here's an example of that for flights from New York City to Rome, Paris and Amsterdam for next year. I wouldn't book any of these because of the high taxes and fees for partner awards, but it at least gives an idea of what's out there. My last suggestion: Keep checking flights in case the price drops. Sometimes, it can make sense to lock in a coach redemption and then keep checking to see if business class opens up at a reasonable rate. If you are willing to be brave, more availability often opens up at the last minute, and you can find some great deals. Related reading:

item.title: Tracing Wild Horse Nine's Filming Locations in Chile: From Santiago to Rapa Nui
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler, Condé Nast Traveler UK
Within minutes of arriving at Ahu Tongariki, an archaeological site on Rapa Nui where 15 massive moai statues face the sea, my guide Gina’s phone alerted with a tsunami warning. She explained that while such alerts are not routine, a 1960 tsunami had previously washed several statues toward the hill. The warning was later lifted, but the moment underscored the fragility of the island’s history. This scene, where the Pacific Ocean looms vast and blue behind the monolithic heads, forms a central motif in *Wild Horse Nine*, a dark comedy directed by Martin McDonagh and filmed partially on Rapa Nui. The film follows two CIA agents, Chris Carlisle (John Malkovich) and Lee Chesterfield (Sam Rockwell), as they travel from Santiago to the Polynesian island for a vacation just before Chile’s 1973 military coup. The event, which ousted socialist president Salvador Allende and installed dictator General Augusto Pinochet, becomes a backdrop to their journey, with the agents’ covert actions hinting at their role in American foreign policy in Latin America. The film’s characters, an acerbic duo reminiscent of McDonagh’s *In Bruges*, embody the detached curiosity of ‘ugly American’ tourists, bristling at attempts to educate them about Rapa Nui’s Indigenous culture. One tourist confronts Chris: ‘Why are you here if you’re just going to make fun of the place?’ Their journey, framed through their eyes, captures both 1970s Santiago and Rapa Nui, blending fiction with historical context. The rising interest in film location tours has led Abercrombie & Kent to launch a nine-day itinerary tracing *Wild Horse Nine*’s route. I traveled to Chile to test this offering, beginning my trip in Santiago, where unseasonable rain obscured the Andes and the Mapocho River threatened to overflow. The 19th-century architecture of Barrio Lastarria, however, remained familiar. My guide, Lisette Matamala, introduced me to the political history underpinning the film’s plot, linking the agents’ mission to the broader tensions of the era. The film’s blend of dark humor and historical intrigue, paired with the real-world significance of its locations, makes the journey both a cinematic and cultural exploration.
